newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian deserter turns to Islam in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russian deserter turns to Islam in Chechnya.

text.p: Twenty-year-old Walid is a model of the new Chechen youth, his dark, wiry frame hardened in war but content now to work on a family hill farm, contemplating his new faith in Islam and learning Arabic.

Like this small Caucasus nation itself, he has undergone a profound transformation from his Soviet past. As the scars of the 21-month war for independence start to heal, he is looking forward to standing on his own two feet after Monday's presidential and parliamentary elections in the region.
That is, Walid would be a model Chechen -- if he were not in fact Russian.

Indeed he is, or was, a Russian soldier called Valentin, one of tens of thousands of poorly-trained conscripts sent up into these mountains by President Boris Yeltsin to do battle with a people of whom they knew nothing but their ferocious, centuries- old desire to be independent of Russia.
"I didn't want to go into the army in the first place," he told Reuters as he chopped wood in a snow-covered field at the weekend. "I didn't know anything about Chechnya."

Walid -- or Valentin -- ran away 18 months ago from what he says were bullying officers and older regular troops of the 506th Motor Rifle Regiment. Before arriving in Chechnya he had never been in a BMP light tank of the type he was supposed to command in battle and had only once fired an automatic rifle.
His bid for freedom took him into the hands of a local band of guerrilla fighters in southern Chechnya and then into the care of the family of one of their commanders.
Unlike some Russian prisoners and deserters, he says he took no part in fighting against his own former comrades.

A year and a half on, Walid is part of the household. He took a Moslem name, speaks the guttural Chechen tongue and has converted to Islam -- indeed, he is more devout than the rest of the family or most Chechens, who barely observe the rituals of the fasting month of Ramadan or abstain from alcohol.
He is learning Arabic, to better understand the Koran.
"It's better here than at home," he said, surveying the crystal clear mountain scenery. It is a far cry from his crumbling industrial hometown in the southern Urals.
Yet for all his disgust with the Russian army and clear admiration for the people who took him in and drove the army out of their homeland, Valentin misses his real family.

Although he thinks his long-term future may lie in Chechnya, Walid would at least like to visit his mother. But she has regular visits from the Russian military commissar, who wants to lock "the deserter" away for a long, long time.
After the horrors of war -- Valentin saw many of his young comrades killed -- his main wish is for peace, and not just within the region but also with Russia.

That is why he says he will vote for Aslan Maskhadov, who commanded of the guerrilla army, in Monday's presidential election, and not for hardline guerrilla leader Shamil Basayev who is a personal friend of the family Walid lives with.
"Maskhadov has more peaceful ideas," he said. "Basayev is more oriented towards war."

Under Maskhadov, Walid hopes, Chechnya, now that it has won its de facto independence, may reconcile itself with its massive and dominant neighbour and start rebuilding its trade and economy from the ruins left by the conflict.

Straw polls suggest Maskhadov is the runaway leader, but if he does not win 50 percent of the vote on Monday, he will need a run-off in two weeks, possibly against Basayev, possibly against the present separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev.

Campaigning was officially banned on Sunday to give the half a million or so voters time to reflect. More than 100 international observers, including Russians, are in the region to monitor the voting. There are 16 presidential candidates and some 850 people seeking 63 seats in a new local assembly.
